panels.figure_caption: EEC syndrome. Stillborn right-hand demonstrates cleft hand.
in_text_mentions: The patient decided on feticide at 22 weeks of gestation. Stillbirth was induced with misoprostol. The patient delivered a male stillborn with multiple dysplasias: absence of the second, third, and fourth fingers on the right hand (Figure 5), presence of the fusions between the first and the second, the third and the fourth toe on the right foot (Figure 6), cleft lip and palate (Figure 7). No other abnormalities were observed, but continued examination was made difficult because of the prematurity of the fetus. No further test was performed at the request of the parents.

This is a real human-patient diagnostic image showing the classic split-hand/lobster-claw manifestation of EEC syndrome; no diagram, control, other disease, or third-party issue is present. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Radiograph of the left hand in a child with EEC syndrome showing absence of the third metacarpal and its phalanges, consistent with central ray deficiency (split-hand/ectrodactyly). Directly captioned as a manifestation of the configured disease. in_text_mentions: In particular, mutations associated with EEC syndrome target the protein’s DNA binding domain, and can occur at various stages of embryonal development [6]. Dysfunctions in p63 contribute to improper epidermal development and differentiation, affecting epidermal lineage commitment, basement membrane deposition and keratinocyte adhesion [7]. In the literature, a plethora of different phenotypes have been reported; however, the most common manifestations are split-hand-split-foot phenotype, defects in tissues of ectodermal origin (skin, hair and teeth), and cleft lip and palate [8,9] (Figure 1).
